content.p: On 10 September 2025 the conservative activist Charlie Kirk, 31, was shot in the neck while answering questions from a crowd at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. A man named Tyler Robinson has been charged with his murder. On 1 September 2026, nearly a year later, a state judge ruled that the evidence was enough to send the case to trial on all seven counts, including aggravated murder, which carries the death penalty in Utah. Robinson, who is now 23, pleaded not guilty through his lawyer. He has not been tried, and everything below about what he did is an allegation by prosecutors, not a finding of guilt.

Kirk had come to Utah to open his American Comeback Tour. Police said about 3,000 people were listening when he was hit. NPR reported that he had been answering a question about transgender perpetrators of mass shootings just before the shot struck him. A campus officer, Christopher Bagley, later told the court that he heard the shot at 12:23 p.m., saw Kirk fall to his left, and watched the crowd run from the tent in the courtyard.

Bagley said he was first told a suspect was already in custody. Then he noticed an empty pistol holder, realised that the sound he had heard was a rifle, and looked across to the roof of the Losee Center, which had a direct line to the courtyard. There he found a red and black screwdriver and a disturbance in the gravel that looked as if someone had lain there. Dispatch found video of a man running toward the roof edge and lying down, then dropping off the north-east side of the building, where Bagley found a shoe imprint. A medical examiner's report, described in court by a state agent, classed the death as a homicide caused by a gunshot wound to the neck.
Kirk was a co-founder of Turning Point USA, a conservative youth organisation active on more than 3,000 college campuses. He left a wife, Erika, and two children aged one and three.

The manhunt lasted about 33 hours, according to NPR. Robinson, then 22 and living in Washington County in the south-west of the state, was taken in on the evening of 11 September after surrendering to the Washington County sheriff. The charging documents, as ABC News reported them, say his mother showed his father the surveillance image released by authorities and the father agreed it looked like their son; he also believed the rifle the police suspected matched one given to his son. NPR said a relative turned him in. According to the charging documents, Robinson told his parents that there was "too much evil" and that Kirk "spreads too much hate", and a family friend who was a deputy sheriff persuaded him to surrender.

On 16 September 2025 Utah County Attorney Jeff Gray announced the charges and said his office would seek the death penalty. He called the killing "an American tragedy" and said he did not take the decision lightly. Robinson appeared by video link from the county jail, said only his name, and was held without bail. He had no defence lawyer at that point.

The charging papers set out what prosecutors say they found. Investigators described a bolt-action rifle recovered the morning after the shooting, which they believe was the murder weapon, and said that casings carried engraved messages, some referring to internet memes and others to anti-fascist slogans. Robinson's mother told investigators he had grown more political and had leaned further left in recent months. The papers also say that on the day of the shooting he texted his roommate and romantic partner to "look under my keyboard", where a note read: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk and I'm going to take it." In later messages, prosecutors say, he wrote "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out," and told the roommate he had been planning for "a little over a week". ABC News reported that Discord confirmed Robinson sent messages admitting responsibility two hours before he was taken into custody.

Prosecutors also charged obstruction and witness tampering. The papers accuse him of disposing of the clothing he wore and of telling the roommate to say nothing to investigators. Prosecutors attached a "victim targeting" enhancement, alleging that Robinson picked Kirk because of Kirk's political expression.

The months before the preliminary hearing were taken up with disputes over publicity and procedure. In October 2025 the defence tried to keep news cameras out of Robinson's hearings, the first of several such efforts that lawyers said were meant to protect his right to a fair trial. Robinson appeared in person for the first time on 11 December 2025. On 3 February 2026 the court heard a defence request to remove the whole Utah County Attorney's Office from the case, because many of its lawyers had relatives or friends at the university that day. The judge denied it, and Utah County still prosecutes. In April 2026 Judge Tony Graf let cameras stay in court but placed limits on filming or photographing Robinson. The defence returned to the issue on the day of the final ruling, citing the publicity and what it called online marketplace gambling tied to the case, and Graf again refused to remove the cameras, subject to his courtroom order.

A Utah defence lawyer who is not involved, Rudy Bautista, told FOX 13 that finding an impartial jury in Utah County would be extremely difficult. He predicted that a trial might not start until September 2029 and could last five to ten weeks. That is his forecast, not a court schedule.

A preliminary hearing asks a narrower question than a trial: whether prosecutors have shown enough evidence to justify sending the charges to a jury. It opened on Monday 6 July 2026 in Provo and was scheduled for five days. Members of Kirk's family, including Erika Kirk, were in the courtroom, and they left when an officer gave the more graphic details of responding to the shooting.

Bagley was the first witness. The second was David Hull, an agent with the Utah Department of Public Safety whose State Bureau of Investigation team took over the inquiry. Hull said he and others reviewed hours of video, that he himself likely watched 10 to 20 hours, and that surveillance footage showed Robinson at the university four times that day. Asked whether the person in the surveillance video was in court, he said yes and described Robinson. The judge refused to admit one recent video because a third party who did not testify had made small alterations to it. Under cross-examination Bagley said he could not identify the person on the roof from the footage, and explained that his body camera had died and he had been too busy to charge it.

Prosecutors also played a recorded interview with the roommate, who did not testify. ABC News reported that he told investigators Robinson confessed in a letter, in text messages and in person. The defence objected to that route, arguing in writing that the state relied on hearsay that was never tested for reliability.

On 1 September 2026 both sides gave closing arguments, and most of the argument was about the aggravating circumstance that makes the case a capital one: that the defendant knowingly created a great risk of death to someone other than the victim.

Deputy County Attorney Ryan McBride said the evidence, including video, clothing and DNA, showed Robinson shot Kirk "because he disagreed with him". He said Robinson went armed to a gathering of more than 3,000 people and, in his words, "didn't care" whom he might hit. McBride added that Robinson "was prepared to take other shots". He pointed to the shooting of President Donald Trump at Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024, where, McBride said, errant bullets hit other people and one was killed, as recent precedent. His colleague Chad Grunander put the distance from the rooftop to Kirk at 415 feet and described a "zone of danger" full of moving people, calling Kirk "a fluid target".

Defence lawyer Staci Visser said the factors for a risk of death to others were "clearly not met". Cases that met it involved multiple shots, verbal threats, pointing a firearm at a bystander or devices likely to injure many people, she said, and here a single shot struck its intended target. She called the prosecution's reasoning about the rifle and the shot's accuracy speculation. Richard Novak argued that nothing showed what Robinson thought of Kirk. The roommate had said, when asked, that he never discussed Kirk with Robinson, Novak said, and he called the state's suggested link to the couple's relationship "an inference without evidence". He also said that a message telling the roommate to ask for a lawyer and stay silent was sent after Robinson had turned himself in and was "altruistic", not obstruction.

Jeff Neiman, a lawyer for the Kirk family, told the court that the family accepted that Robinson was entitled to a fair trial, but wanted it held without delay. "The right to delay is not among them," he said of the rights the Constitution gives defendants.

Graf announced his decision after 6 p.m. local time. "Viewed in the light most favorable to the prosecution, this evidence is sufficient at this stage to support a reasonable belief the defendant is the individual who shot and killed Charlie Kirk," he said. He stressed that the standard was not proof beyond a reasonable doubt. "Whether the state can prove the aggravating circumstance beyond a reasonable doubt remains for trial," he said, and he found probable cause for both the risk-of-death circumstance and the victim-targeting allegation. All seven counts were bound over: aggravated murder and felony discharge of a firearm, both first-degree felonies; two counts of obstruction of justice, second-degree felonies; two counts of witness tampering, third-degree felonies; and committing a violent offense in the presence of a child, a Class A misdemeanor.
The court moved straight to arraignment. The defence waived a formal reading of the charges, and Robinson's lawyer entered not guilty pleas for him.

Kirk's family said in a statement that the ruling was an important step in their "pursuit of justice" and asked for "a transparent and timely process". Outside, a small group of students from the university's Turning Point chapter waited quietly to support the family.

Robinson is due back in court at 1 p.m. on 23 October 2026 for a status conference, and the judge has told the lawyers to be ready to propose trial dates. The family's lawyer has asked that a date be set then. Graf has left it to a trial to decide if the aggravating circumstance is proved to the higher standard.
